title: Daily reading
tomorrow: Dad says sadaqah has to be money. what if you're broke till payday?

cards: New-year plans have a way of dying in the first week: the gym, the journal, the whole Qur'an over winter break. It's day four, and the plan is three days behind. Quit, or cram?
Here's something odd in the Qur'an itself. Surah al-Muzzammil opens by asking the Prophet ﷺ to stand much of the night in prayer and recitation.
Then its last verse, one long verse, says the same short thing twice: recite of the Qur'an what is easy for you. Why say it twice?

teach.b: Read what sits between the two.
In the middle of that verse, the Qur'an names the reasons a long night of reading won't always fit: some of you are sick, some travel the land looking for a living, some are fighting in God's cause.
Real lives, named one by one.
Then, again: so recite of it what is easy. The repeat isn't a typo. It's the ease arriving after the reasons, so nobody misses it.
That's the root of a wird: a daily portion, a set amount of Qur'an someone returns to every day. A page, a few verses, a section.
In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet says the deeds most loved by God are the ones done most constantly, even if they're small. And there's a story about pushing too hard.

A young companion, Abdullah ibn Amr, was reading the whole Qur'an every night. The Prophet told him once a month. Abdullah bargained for more, and more, until the Prophet said: then in seven, and no faster.

teach.h: ABDULLAH WISHED HE'D TAKEN IT EASY.
teach.b: Years later, an old man, Abdullah said he wished he'd accepted the easier one. So the puzzle has an answer for day four. Not quit, not cram.
Make the portion smaller, and make it daily.

how: Muslims who keep a wird, a fixed daily portion of the Qur'an, often read a page or a section after Fajr or before sleep; printed copies are divided into parts that make a steady pace easy to track.

o: a verse memorized once and recited only at funerals
a reading of the whole Qur'an in a single night
a daily portion of Qur'an that someone keeps every day

games.q: the daily portion — tap the pairs.
p: the most constant, even if small
wished he'd taken the easier pace

s: one verse of al-Muzzammil says 'recite what is easy' twice
first the ease, then the reasons (sickness, travel for a living, fighting), then the ease again.
Abdullah ibn Amr was glad all his life that he pushed for a faster pace
as an old man he said he wished he'd accepted the easier one.
a wird has to be long to count
the deeds most loved by God are the most constant, even if small.

games.q: your dad works twelve-hour days at his shop and wants to start reading Qur'an daily. he asks you what a realistic wird is.
o: a big section a day, so he finishes fast and feels it.
nothing until the shop slows down and he has real time.
a page or a few verses he can keep every single day.
games.why: the verse names real lives, work included, and says recite what is easy. small and constant is what the hadith says God loves.

practice: Open whatever you read from, a Qur'an, a translation, any book you keep coming back to, and choose one short line. Read it out loud, slowly, then once more even slower. Then sit with the second reading still in your ears.

wordCard.voice: Wird: a daily portion, a set amount someone returns to every day. Small enough to keep, kept every day.

orig.note: Arabic: a regular portion, a set amount of Qur'an or dhikr kept daily.

carryVoice: Your line: my portion, small enough to keep and kept daily. Day four of a plan isn't the end of it. Nine of fourteen.

sources.ref: Qur'an 73:1–4, 73:20 (stand much of the night; recite of the Qur'an what is easy, said twice in 73:20)
Sahih al-Bukhari 6464 (the most beloved deeds to God are the most constant, even if small)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5052, 5054 (Abdullah ibn Amr: finish in a month, bargained to seven; his regret in old age)
